ducts his work. Such is the idea of Cefar, which a
painter has in his mind when he goes to make a picture

<x_0.7324><y_0.0328>Exemplification
Exercife.<x_0.8457><y_0.0883><class_Picture>

<x_0.0342><y_0.0844>EXEMPLIFICATION _of Letters Patent_, denotes
an examplan, or copy of letters patent, made from the
enrolment thereof, and fealed with the great feal of
England. Such exemplifications are as effectual to be
thowed or pleaded, as the letters patent themfelves.<x_0.7305><y_0.1531><class_Text>

<x_0.0322><y_0.1523>EXEMPTION, in _Law_, a privilege to be free from
fome service or appearance: thus, barons and peers of
the realm are, on account of their dignity, exempted
from being fworn upon inquefts; and knights, clergy-
men, and others, from appearing at the heriff's turn.
Perfons of 70 years of age, apothecaries, &c. are alfo
by law exempted from ferving on juries; and juiltices of
the peace, attorneys, &c. from parish offices.<x_0.7295><y_0.2594><class_Text>

<x_0.0312><y_0.2578>EXERCISE, among physicians, fuch an agitation
of the body as produces futulary effects in the animal
economy.<x_0.7285><y_0.2984><class_Text>

<x_0.0303><y_0.2977>Exercife may be laid to be either active or pallive.
The active is walking, hunting, dancing, playing at
bowls, and the like; as alfo freaking, and other la-
bour of the body and mind. The palive is riding in
a coach, on horleback, or in any other manner. Ex-
ercife may be continued to a beginning of wearinels,
and ought to be ufed before dinner in a pure light
air; for which reafon, journeys, and going into the
country, contribute greatly to preserve and re-eltablith
health.<x_0.7275><y_0.4305><class_Text>

<x_0.0273><y_0.4313>Exercife increases the circulation of the blood, atte-
nuates and divides the fluids, and promotes a regular
perfpiration, as well as a due feeretion of all the hu-
mours; for it accelerates the animal fpirits, and facili-
tates their distribution into all the fibres of the body,
flrengthens the parts, creates an appetite, and helps di-
getition. Whence it arises, that those who accullom
themelves to exercite are generally very robust, and fel-
dom subject to difeafes.<x_0.7266><y_0.5516><class_Text>

<x_0.0225><y_0.5523>Boerhaave recommends bodily exercise in difeafes of
a weak and lax fibre. By riding on horfeback, fays
his commentator, the pendulous vifcera of the abdo-
med are flaken every moment, and gently rubbed as
it were one against another, while in the mean time the
pure air acts on the lungs with greater force. But it is
to be obferved that a weak man should not ride with a
full stomach, but either before dinner, or after the di-
getion is nearly finished; for when the flowach is di-
lended, weak people do not bear thefe concullions of
the horfe without difficulty; but when the prime vice
are nearly empty, the remaining feces are discharged by
this concuffion. Salling in a hip is alfo an exercice of
great ufe to weak people. If the veffel moves with an
even motion, by increasing peripiration it ufually ex-
cites a wonderful alacrity, creates an appetite, and pro-
motes digestion. These exercises are more especially
serviceable to weak people; but, in order to flrengthen
the body by muscular motion, running and bodily ex-
ercifes are to be ufed. In thefe we thould begin with
the moft gentle, fuch as walking, and increate it by de-
grees till we come to running. Thofe exercifes of the
body are more efpecially ferviceable which give delight
to the mind at the fame time, as tennis, fencing, &c.;
for which reafon, the wifdom of antiquity appointed
rewards for thofe who excelled in thefe gymnastic ex-
ercifes.<x_0.7256><y_0.9141><class_Text>
